Because that corridor accounts for the journey, all links were recorded as confident rather than capped at probable.

One thing worth looking into next: Sarah Pratt, who appears in the 1860 household at age 13, is absent from the 1880 household — she would have been about 33 by then. She may have married and been enumerated under a married surname, died before 1880, or been living elsewhere. Searching for a marriage record or later census entry for Sarah Pratt in Utah (or a nearby territory) in the 1860s and 1870s would help account for her.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

---

## Review of pe_005: a_013 → Patrick Flynn (I1), confidence `confident`

**What this link claims**

pe_005 asserts that the "deceased" role in death certificate record `ark:/61903/1:1:MDEF` is Patrick Flynn (I1), based on assertion a_013 — the relationship claim on that certificate stating "Father: Thomas Flynn."

---

### Confidence calibration assessment

The recorded confidence of `confident` is **defensible on the identity question itself**, but the rationale as written does not adequately support or justify it. Two concerns:

**The identity conclusion is likely sound.** The death certificate states death on 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. The tree already carries I1's Death fact (F2) with exactly that date and place, sourced to the same Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection (S3) — a precise two-part match on primary information. No other Patrick Flynn is known in the county at that time.

**The rationale, however, is thin to the point of being an inadequate audit trail.** Four specific problems:

1. **Both mandatory check lines are absent.** There is no documented date check ("record birth year vs. tree birth year") or residence check ("record place vs. nearest attested residence"). A reviewer reading pe_005 in isolation has no documented basis for the tier.

2. **The birthplace discrepancy is not acknowledged.** Assertion a_012 from the same persona notes the death certificate gives birthplace as Pennsylvania, while census records give Ireland. The same informant — James Brown, son-in-law, `family_not_present` — provided both a_012 and a_013. His known inaccuracy on birthplace is directly relevant to assessing the reliability of a_013's parentage claim, and it should be named in the rationale.

3. **`match_score` is null with no explanation.** The null may predate enforcement rules, but the rationale should explain why no score is present rather than leaving the field silent.

4. **The rationale does not engage with corroboration.** Two prior census records (1850, 1860) already confidently place Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County under Thomas Flynn's household. Those links are the strongest corroborating context and belong in the rationale.

---

### Additional observation

Assertions a_011 (the death fact, primary informant) and a_012 (the birth fact, secondary informant) from this same persona have **no `pe_` entries at all** — an unlinked-assertion gap worth addressing as a follow-up.

---

### Recommended improved rationale

The tier can stay at `confident`, but the rationale should be rewritten:

> *"Date check: record gives birth year 1845 (via secondary informant, son-in-law); tree person born ~1845 (from 1850 census): gap 0 years, consistent. Note: the same death certificate reports birthplace as Pennsylvania (a_012), conflicting with Ireland established by the 1850 census — the informant (James Brown, son-in-law, family not present) is demonstrably unreliable on this point; this does not affect the identity conclusion but reduces the evidential weight of a_013's parentage claim. Residence check: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1908 vs. prior attested residence Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1860 census): same county, no move to explain. Death date 12 March 1908 is primary information (attending physician) and an exact match to the tree person's established Death fact (F2). Name and death place match. Thomas Flynn named as father is consistent with 1850 and 1860 census links already established. ---

### Summary

The `confident` tier is **defensible but not well documented**. As written, pe_005 would not pass a GPS audit — no date check, no residence check, no acknowledgment of the informant's known inaccuracy, and a silent null score. The tier itself does not need to change; the rationale does.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The skill violated the decided rule by assigning 'confident' confidence to the 1880 census links (pe_012–pe_022). The rule explicitly caps unexplained transatlantic moves at 'probable' and forbids 'confident'. The skill's rationale for the 1880 links claims the 1870 census 'bridges the move,' but a single intermediate census in the same destination county does not bridge a transatlantic move from Sussex to Tennessee with no passenger list, naturalization, or emigration record in the project. The 1870 census establishes continuity within Tennessee, not the transatlantic crossing. The 1870 links are correctly marked 'probable,' but the 1880 links are factually incorrect in their confidence tier.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The skill addressed all required work: extracted and linked all 11 assertions from the 1870 census and all 9 from the 1880 census to the correct tree persons (I1–I5), created 22 person_evidence entries, materialized facts into the tree for all household members, and checked for genealogical warnings. No required assertions or persons were omitted.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed arguments matching the fixture's expected_args semantically. place_search, place_distance, and wiki_read were invoked correctly to measure the geographic gap and check for a corridor. same_person was called for each assertion with a tree candidate, with correct recordRole parameters for relationship assertions' second parties. No critical identifiers were wrong, and no calls landed in fixture_not_found.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: The 1870 census links (pe_001–pe_011) are correctly marked 'probable' with rationales naming the geographic gap (6804 km, no documentary bridge, no corridor). However, the 1880 census links (pe_012–pe_022) are marked 'confident' in violation of the decided rule. The skill claims the 1870 census 'bridges the move,' but a single intermediate record in the same destination county does not bridge an unexplained transatlantic move. The rule forbids 'confident' on such moves; the skill's confidence tier for the 1880 links is factually incorrect.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: The 1870 rationales cite specific matching attributes (name, age, birth year, birthplace, household composition) and explicitly name the geographic gap (6804 km, no documentary bridge, no corridor). However, the 1880 rationales claim the 1870 census 'bridges the move' without explaining why a single intermediate census in the same destination county would resolve a transatlantic move with no passenger list or naturalization record. The rationales do not adequately justify the upgrade from 'probable' to 'confident' or address why the absence of a documented crossing is no longer a constraint.

dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
dimensions.rationale: All relationship assertions are linked to both parties. The 1880 wife assertion (a_019) is linked to both I2 (primary, pe_019) and I1 (second party, pe_020). The son assertion (a_020) is linked to both I5 (primary, pe_021) and I1 (second party, pe_022). Both sides of each relationship are represented in the person_evidence entries.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
dimensions.rationale: No new persons were minted; all five household members already existed in the tree. The skill correctly used materialize_facts to enrich existing persons with sourced facts from both census records. Facts were written with source references (S10 for 1870, S11 for 1880). No edges needed to be written because this is a non-household record scenario (census records are household records, but the skill correctly linked existing persons rather than creating new ones). The merge_warnings gate was not required because no new persons were being materialized.

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for every assertion with a tree candidate. Each call correctly scored the record persona against the tree person (all returned 0.78). The scores were recorded in match_score and informed the confidence tier (capping at 'probable' for the 1870 links due to the geographic gap, not the score). The score did not override correlation; the geographic constraint was the controlling factor, as required.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: All 22 person_evidence entries were created with factually correct data. Names, ages, birth years, and places match the tree persons and census records. Confidence levels are correctly calibrated to 'probable' across all entries, reflecting the geographic cap rule: the move from Horsham, Sussex to Maury County, Tennessee (~6804 km) is unexplained by any documentary bridge or corridor, so 'confident' is appropriately rejected. Rationales consistently name the geographic gap (both places, distance, and absence of bridge). The materialize_facts calls correctly enriched existing persons with residence facts from both censuses. No fabricated material or unsupported claims.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: All five household members from both the 1870 and 1880 censuses were linked to the correct tree persons. The 1870 census yielded 11 person_evidence entries (5 persons × 2 facts + 1 residence for William); the 1880 census yielded 11 entries (William, Mary, George with facts and relationships, plus relationship assertions linking both parties). All assertions from both sources were addressed. The household absence of James and Ellen in 1880 was flagged as a follow-up item. No required work was omitted.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed arguments matching expected values. research_query calls for src_001 and src_002 correctly retrieved assertions. tree_query for I1–I5 retrieved the correct persons and relationships. place_search calls for 'Maury County, Tennessee' and 'Horsham, Sussex, England' matched expected place names. place_distance correctly measured the two standardized places. wiki_read correctly targeted Tennessee_Emigration_and_Immigration. same_person calls correctly paired each assertion with its tree person, using recordRole only for the second party of relationship assertions (a_019 and a_020 with I1 as head). research_append and materialize_facts calls were well-formed. No fixture_not_found errors; all calls succeeded.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All 22 person_evidence entries are scored 'probable', which is correct. The rule cap applies: the record place (Maury County, Tennessee) is outside the attested residence cluster (Horsham, Sussex, England 1851–1861), and no documentary bridge (passenger list, naturalization, emigration record) or corridor (Tennessee_Emigration_and_Immigration names pre-statehood overland settlers from Virginia/Carolinas, not Sussex in the 1860s) explains the move. A single census would be 'probable' at best; two independent censuses corroborate the identity but do not lift it past the geographic cap. No entry claims 'confident', and no entry incorrectly claims 'speculative'. The confidence tier matches the evidence strength.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites specific matching attributes: name (exact match), age (gap 0 years), birth year (~1825, ~1828, etc.), birthplace (England), and household position (head, household_member_1, wife, son). Rationales address the geographic gap explicitly, naming both places (Maury, Tennessee vs. Horsham, Sussex, England), the distance (6804 km), and the absence of a documentary bridge or corridor. Rationales note corroboration across two censuses where applicable (e.g., George Weller in both 1870 and 1880). Disambiguation is implicit in the household context: all five members match by name, age, and relationship, ruling out competing candidates. Rationales are substantive, not generic.

dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
dimensions.rationale: Relationship assertions in the 1880 census (wife-of-William, son-of-William) were linked on both sides. a_019 (wife relationship) generated pe_017 (I2) and pe_018 (I1); a_020 (son relationship) generated pe_021 (I5) and pe_022 (I1). Each relationship-implying assertion has person_evidence entries for both parties. The 1870 census household members were linked individually without explicit relationship assertions in the extracted data, but the rationales note the known ParentChild edges (R2–R7) from the tree, confirming awareness of the multi-person structure.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
dimensions.rationale: No new persons were minted; all five tree persons (I1–I5) pre-existed. materialize_facts was called twice (once for the 1870 census, once for the 1880 census) to enrich existing persons with sourced residence facts and name references. The tool responses confirm facts were added/enriched and refs attached (e.g., I1 received 1 fact added, 1 enriched, 3 refs attached from the 1870 census). No edges were written via tree_edit because the household relationships (Couple R1, ParentChild R2–R7) were already established in the tree from the 1851 and 1861 English censuses. This is correct: edges are owed only when a household record introduces new persons or relationships; here all persons and edges pre-existed. No person was overwritten or renamed. Confidence is calibrated to the evidence (probable, not confident).

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was invoked for every tree candidate in play: a_001, a_003, a_005, a_007, a_009 (1870 census personas CP1–CP5 vs. I1–I5); a_012, a_014, a_016, a_019 (1880 census personas DP1–DP3 vs. I1, I2, I5); and a_019, a_020 with recordRole for the second party (I1 as head). Each call returned a score of 0.78, which was recorded in match_score and informed the confidence decision (probable, not confident, despite the high score, because the geographic gap caps it). The score was not allowed to override the geographic constraint. For relationship assertions, the first party's persona was not reused for the second party; separate calls with recordRole were made (a_019 with I1 as head; a_020 with I1 as head). The score is treated as an input that informs, not replaces, the correlation analysis.

The family's last attested residence before the census was **Horsham, Sussex, England** — roughly 6,800 km from Maury County, Tennessee. Search for a passenger arrival or naturalization record documenting the Wellers' immigration from England to Tennessee between 1861 and 1870. Finding that record would lift all links to **confident** and also help explain what happened to James and Ellen.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed correct arguments. same_person was called for each assertion with matching tree person (assertionId and treePersonId correct; recordRole supplied for second-party links on relationship assertions). place_search was called for both Horsham and Maury County with appropriate place names. place_distance received standardized place names from the search results. wiki_read was called with the correct Tennessee emigration URL. research_append and materialize_facts calls were properly structured. No fixture_not_found errors occurred. A single validation rejection on the first research_append batch was competently recovered: the agent called same_person for a_019 and a_020 as instructed, then resubmitted with correct match_scores.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All 22 links are scored 'probable', which is correct. The rule cap applies: a single strong source (0.78 same_person score, matching names/ages/children across two independent censuses) with no corroborating bridge document is 'probable' at best. The geographic gap (6,804 km, no passenger list, naturalization, or corridor documented) prevents 'confident'. The rationale for each link explicitly names the gap: 'Maury County, Tennessee, 1870 vs nearest attested Horsham, Sussex, England, 1861: outside, 6804 km; no corridor or bridge' or similar. The skill consulted the Tennessee emigration wiki and correctly found no qualifying sentence naming England with an arrival verb for the 1861–1870 era. This is neither 'speculative' (which would over-apply the rule) nor 'confident' (which would ignore the gap). The confidence tier matches the identity-evidence strength.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites multiple specific matching attributes: name (exact match), age (consistent with tree birth year, gap 0 years), birthplace (England matches), and household position (enumerated as head, wife, son, etc., consistent with tree relationships). The geographic gap is explicitly addressed in every rationale with measured distance (6,804 km), the two places named, and the absence of a documentary bridge or corridor stated. The rationale explains why the link is probable rather than confident: the move is unexplained. Competing candidates are not an issue here (the household is small and names are distinctive), but the skill does address why the strong correlation does not elevate to confident.

dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness

All parent-child and couple relationships (R1–R7) already existed in the tree; the skill did not write new edges because the household skeleton was already complete. materialize_facts was called for both the 1870 and 1880 records, enriching each person with residence and birth facts sourced to the census records. No conflicts were surfaced. The skill correctly did not attempt to mint new persons or write redundant edges.

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for every assertion with a tree candidate in play. The score (0.78, strong band >0.7) was recorded in match_score and informed the confidence decision without overriding it: the high score did not auto-elevate to 'confident' because the geographic gap contradicts it. The score was treated as input that informs correlation analysis, not as the verdict. For relationship assertions (a_019, a_020), the second party's recordRole (head) was supplied to ensure the score compared the right record party (DP1 vs I1, not DP2 or DP3 vs I1).
